introduction-your-private-slice-of-the-c.core: A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network in a cloud region: you choose its IP range (CIDR), carve it into subnets per availability zone, and control routing, internet access and security. Nothing enters or leaves unless you configure it (gateways, routes, security rules), which makes the VPC the foundation of cloud network security and connectivity design.

first_principles.problem: A team launches everything in the default VPC with public IPs and later can't segment or connect it to the corporate network.
truths: IP ranges must not overlap if networks connect.

analogy.title: A private gated estate
analogy.story: You own the land plan, decide the streets (subnets), the gates (gateways) and the guards (security groups).
analogy.breaks: Estates can't be cloned in minutes; VPCs can, so plan IP ranges for growth.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Isolated network; nothing reachable until configured.

check.q: Why does CIDR choice matter at VPC creation?
check.a: Overlapping ranges prevent peering/VPN/TGW connectivity later, and changing a VPC's primary CIDR is disruptive.

subnetting-cidr-math-the-basics.core: CIDR notation /n means the first n bits are the network; the remaining 32−n bits give 2^(32−n) addresses. A /16 is 65,536 addresses, a /24 is 256, and in AWS 5 addresses per subnet are reserved. You split a VPC CIDR into subnets by borrowing bits: a /16 splits into 256 /24s or 16 /20s. Plan for growth and leave room for future AZs and tiers.

first_principles.problem: A VPC built with /28 subnets runs out of IPs when EKS assigns a pod IP to every pod.

analogy.title: Dividing a plot of land into lots
analogy.story: Each extra bit halves the lot size and doubles the number of lots.
analogy.breaks: Land can be re-surveyed; subnet CIDRs can't be resized in place.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Large private subnets for pods, small public ones for LBs.

check.q: How many usable IPs does an AWS /24 subnet have?

availability-zones-and-multi-az-vpc-desi.core: An availability zone is one or more data centres with independent power and networking; a region has several. Subnets live in exactly one AZ, so high availability means spreading every tier across at least two (better three) AZs, with load balancers, Multi-AZ databases and per-AZ NAT gateways, so losing one AZ doesn't take down the service.

first_principles.problem: An AZ outage takes down production because all app instances and the NAT gateway were in us-east-1a.
derivation: Deploy **NAT per AZ** with per-AZ routes.

analogy.title: Keeping spare keys at different friends' houses
analogy.story: If one friend is away, another can let you in.
analogy.breaks: Friends are independent; cross-AZ traffic costs money and latency.

example.title: Three-AZ layout
flow: Each private route table → own AZ's NAT

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any single AZ can fail with service intact.

check.q: Why deploy a NAT gateway in each AZ?
check.a: A single NAT gateway is an AZ-level single point of failure; per-AZ NATs with per-AZ routes keep egress working if one AZ fails.

internet-gateway-and-route-tables-the-tr.core: Route tables decide where traffic goes: each subnet is associated with one, and the most specific matching route wins. The 'local' route covers the VPC CIDR. A subnet is public only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway (and instances need public IPs); a private subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway or nowhere. The IGW also performs 1:1 NAT for public IPs.

first_principles.problem: An instance with a public IP can't reach the internet because its subnet's route table has no IGW route.
truths: Subnets are public only by routing.

analogy.title: Signposts at an estate's junctions
analogy.story: Streets with a sign to the main gate are 'public'; others only lead to the service exit or stay internal.
analogy.breaks: Signposts guide people; routes are enforced for every packet.

check.q: What makes a subnet 'public' in AWS?
check.a: Its route table has a route for 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway.

nat-gateways-vs-instances.core: Private instances need outbound internet (updates, APIs) without being reachable inbound. NAT translates their private source IPs to a public IP. Managed NAT gateways are highly available within an AZ, scale automatically and need no patching, but charge per hour and per GB processed. NAT instances are cheaper at low volume but are single points of failure you must maintain. For AWS services, VPC endpoints avoid NAT entirely.

first_principles.problem: A NAT gateway processing 50 TB/month of S3 traffic costs $2,250 in data processing alone.
truths: Managed services trade cost for operations.

analogy.title: A company switchboard for outgoing calls
analogy.story: Staff can call out, showing the main number; outsiders can't dial staff extensions directly.
analogy.breaks: Switchboards don't charge per word; NAT gateways charge per GB.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: S3 traffic no longer billed through NAT.

check.q: How do you avoid NAT gateway processing charges for S3 traffic?
check.a: Use an S3 gateway VPC endpoint, which routes S3 traffic privately with no per-GB charge.

security-groups-and-network-acls-two-lay.core: Security groups are stateful firewalls attached to network interfaces: allow-only rules, and return traffic is automatically permitted. They can reference other security groups instead of IPs. Network ACLs are stateless filters at the subnet boundary with ordered allow and deny rules, so they need explicit return-traffic rules (ephemeral ports). Use SGs as the primary control and NACLs for coarse subnet-level denies.

first_principles.problem: A NACL allowing inbound 443 breaks HTTPS because return traffic on ephemeral ports isn't allowed outbound.
truths: Stateless filters see each packet alone.
Identity-based rules scale better than IPs.

analogy.title: A doorman vs a checkpoint
analogy.story: The doorman (SG) remembers who went out and lets them back in; the checkpoint (NACL) checks every person both ways against a list.
analogy.breaks: Doormen can be persuaded; rules are exact.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only the ALB can reach app port, whatever their IPs.

code.text:
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "app_from_alb" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  ip_protocol = "tcp"
  from_port   = 8080
  to_port     = 8080
}

check.q: Why must NACLs allow ephemeral ports for return traffic?
check.a: NACLs are stateless, so responses to allowed requests (sent to client ephemeral ports) need their own explicit allow rules.

bastion-hosts-the-jump-box.core: A bastion (jump host) is a hardened instance in a public subnet that admins SSH into before hopping to private hosts. It shrinks the exposed surface to one host, but it's still an internet-facing SSH server with keys to manage. Modern alternatives remove inbound access entirely: AWS SSM Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, or identity-aware proxies with short-lived credentials and full session logging.

first_principles.problem: A bastion with SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 and shared keys is brute-forced and becomes an entry point.
derivation: If bastion: **restrict source IPs**, MFA, hardened AMI.

analogy.title: A guarded side entrance vs a remote-unlock system
analogy.story: The guarded door is better than none, but a system that issues one-time passes with CCTV is better still.
analogy.breaks: Guards can be bribed; SSM removes the door entirely.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: SSM gives shell with IAM auth and CloudTrail/S3 logs.

code.text:
# bastion
ssh -J ec2-user@bastion.example.com ec2-user@10.20.3.14
# no inbound ports at all
aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123def456

check.q: What's the main security advantage of SSM Session Manager over a bastion?
check.a: No inbound ports or SSH keys are needed; access uses IAM and every session is logged.

vpc-peering-and-the-transitive-limitatio.core: VPC peering connects two VPCs privately over the provider backbone with no bandwidth bottleneck. It's non-transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C through B, and an edge VPC can't share its IGW or VPN with peers. CIDRs must not overlap, and route tables on both sides need routes. With many VPCs, a full mesh needs n(n−1)/2 peerings, which is why hub-and-spoke Transit Gateways exist.

first_principles.problem: Ten VPCs require 45 peering connections and route entries, and nobody can track them.

analogy.title: Private footbridges between neighbouring houses
analogy.story: You can walk to your neighbour's, but not through their house to the next street.
analogy.breaks: Footbridges are physical; peering is just routing, but equally non-transitive.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Peering doesn't scale to many VPCs.

check.q: If A peers with B and B peers with C, can A reach C?
check.a: No, peering is non-transitive; A needs its own peering with C or a transit gateway.
